headline: Execution Rocks goes dark-hours only — bass feeding on chunks after 10 PM
subhead: Daytime marks have gone quiet in the warm water, but the after-dark bite at the Rocks and the Throgs Neck rip is putting real fish in the boat.
body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island Avenue asked me Tuesday why his sounder's been showing nothing but bait balls and empty water at Execution Rocks in the middle of the day. Told him the same thing I've told a hundred guys this time of year — the bass haven't left, they've just gone to work the night shift. Kings Point is reading just under 71 degrees right now, and once the surface gets into the low 70s like this, stripers in the Western Sound stop cruising the flats at noon and start stacking up deep on structure, waiting for dark. That's not a theory, that's thirty years of watching the same pattern play out every July.

So if you want bass this week, you fish the clock, not the calendar. Execution Rocks on the last two hours of the outgoing, after 9 or 10 at night, has been the most consistent thing going. I had a report of a 28-pounder taken on a bunker chunk fished on the bottom in about 22 feet just off the rockpile, current still running hard. Eels work too — snag one live off the reef, drift it back with the tide, and let it swim naturally past the rocks. The fish are sitting tight to structure waiting for the current to push bait past them, and they're not moving much to chase it, so slow presentations right on the bottom are outfishing anything fast.

Stepping Stones is doing the same thing on the front half of the incoming, right around the light. That rip has been a spring highway for years, and it doesn't fully shut down in summer — it just moves its hours. Bunker chunks, fresh not frozen, fished right in the seam where the current breaks off the light structure. Throgs Neck Bridge is holding fish too, mostly on the pilings closest to the Bronx side where the tide rips hardest — that's a night bite as well, live eels drifted along the base of the piers on the last two hours of the ebb.

Bluefish are the one thing still willing to show up in daylight, and they've been reliable. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bluefish bite would hold through the weekend as long as conditions stayed warm and stable, and that's exactly what's playing out. Bunker schools are stacked up off Matinecock Point in good numbers, and the blues are riding right underneath them. Poppers and bunker spoons in the early morning when the school gets nervous and starts flipping on top — that's your window, usually the first hour of light before the boat traffic pushes everything down. Metal, like a Kastmaster or an Ava jig, worked through the edges of the school will connect too if the topwater bite doesn't materialize.

Fluke have thinned out on the open flats — that shallow, warm water isn't holding them the way it did in June. The fish that are left have pushed into the deeper channel edges and current-swept structure, which around here means the Hart Island channel and the deeper water off the Throgs Neck approach. Four to six pound fish are still coming out of there on white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming when the current's still got some push to it but isn't ripping. It's not the volume bite it was a month ago — you're working for quality now, not quantity, and I'd rather cover less water slower than blind-drift the flats hoping for a stray.

Porgies are still an honest bite around the reef structure off City Island and out toward the western edge of the Sound — bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig, bottom fished on the slower stages of the tide, gives you a box of fish without much fuss if you want dinner and don't want to think too hard about it. Weakfish have been quiet, but I've had a couple reports of fish coming from the deeper holes near Hart Island after dark on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid — worth a shot but don't build a trip around it.

Moon's waxing toward full in the first days of August, which means the current through Stepping Stones and the Rocks is going to get stronger through this week and next. That's good news for the night bass bite — stronger current concentrates bait tighter against structure, and these fish don't have to work as hard to eat. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd take the outgoing at Execution Rocks starting two hours before low, bunker chunk on the bottom, and I'd be patient. This isn't a run-and-gun bite right now. It's a sit-still-and-wait-for-dark bite, and the guys putting in the hours after sundown are the ones filling coolers while everybody else wonders where the fish went.
